overview.text: The Bridegroom is the title used in the Holy Week services of the first three days. GOARCH relates it to the Bridegroom in the parable of the Ten Virgins and to Christ’s Passion and Second Coming.
overview.reason: Necessary concise account of a modern published source; substantial verbatim reproduction is not licensed. This is an editorial summary, not the source author’s wording.

blocks.text: GOARCH describes the icon as Christ during his mockery by soldiers: crowned with thorns, clothed in purple and holding a reed. This is the humiliated King during the Passion, with the Gospel’s royal title turned into the soldiers’ taunt.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of a modern published source; substantial verbatim reproduction is not licensed. This is an editorial summary, not the source author’s wording.

blocks.text: The pictured historical Greek icon is identified as Christ the Bridegroom from Saint Paraskevi Church in Langadas. Its surviving painted surface visibly includes the thorn-crowned Christ and the identifying Greek title; losses in the paint have not been reconstructed.

blocks.text: The archdiocesan explanation associates the Bridegroom imagery with the union of Christ and the Church and the expectation of his return. The evening services from Palm Sunday through Holy Tuesday are the Orthros of the following day.

blocks.text: And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him. Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.
